pair_redecisions.reason: The selected part (c) asks total distance on 0..3 after the velocity/rest event have been recovered. It must recognise the interior reversal at 2 and add |integral 0..2v|+|integral 2..3 v|. The target supplies v=30exp(-t/2)>0 and needs only integral 0..2v. This is a harder motion-distance branch because of the sign-change split; the unrelated maximum/velocity-at 3 responses are not compared.

Part (c-i) integrates the previously recovered v=10t+8 and fixes s(0)=0 at the shaft top; (c-ii) evaluates that displacement at the stated 4 s to give depth. The target integrates its supplied positive velocity from the start to a stated 2 s. Both give distance with no reversal or event-time solving. The source’s explicit displacement expression is the intermediate indefinite-integral route to the same numeric motion response, not a requirement to solve the unrelated top event in Example 39.

Selected Example 39(b) integrates the already stated signed acceleration -10 and determines its constant from v(0)=12, establishing v=12-10t. The target integrates a=6t+1 and determines its constant from v(0)=2, returning v(t). Constant versus linear acceleration is a power-rule variation; the source show-that form retains the same method. Its later height/top-event parts are excluded.

Selected Example 38(d) asks the distance travelled in the first 2 s from given v=12t-t²; v is nonnegative on 0..2 and its single definite integral gives 64/3 m. The target uses the same fixed interval, given one-signed velocity, motion interpretation and numeric distance response. The source’s acceleration, maximum and next-rest parts are not selected.

Selected Try Now 39 Q1(c-i, c-ii) integrates the previous velocity, uses displacement0 at t=0, then evaluates at the specified4s to obtain shaft depth. The target uses its previous positive velocity and displacement0 atO to obtain distance after3s. Both are the same polynomial velocity-to-displacement and fixed-time evaluation sequence; upward/downward context and polynomial degree do not add a different learner decision. No greatest-height event is selected.

Both obtain dy/dx by dividing parameter derivatives and use it to form a tangent at a particular parameter. Example22 supplies t=3; the exam first solves y=t(1+t)=0 to obtain two contact parameters and must return both tangents. That contact-point selection and repeated tangent output makes the selected textbook response easier. The general tangent in ii is source scaffolding, and elimination/sketch iv is excluded.

Both differentiate each parameter coordinate and form dy/dx. Q15(i) uses chain differentiation on cubic trigonometric coordinates and returns the general formula -tan t. The exam differentiates an exponential coordinate and the product 4t²e^(-t), then evaluates the quotient at the iterated parameter from (b) and rounds to 2 significant figures. The absent product-rule/exponential derivative and inherited numerical evaluation make the selected textbook subpart easier; its tangent/intercept follow-ups are excluded.

Both use trigonometric parameter derivatives and dy/dx=(dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ). Example23(i) gives the general gradient -3cosθ/(4sinθ) for elementary trig coordinates. The exam has a sum containing cos2θ, so its x derivative needs a chain factor, and it requires the numerical value at θ=1 radian. Those extra derivative/evaluation demands make the selected textbook subpart easier. The normal, coordinate and sketch parts ii–v are excluded.

The domain bullet explicitly asks for justification that y=log_a x exists only when x>0; explaining x=a^y>0 supplies the shared positive-argument principle. The exam applies it to ln(x-2) and requests the single numerical cutoff 2. The source requires an explanation of the basic graph, while the target adds an affine input shift and gives a numerical boundary, so this is a mixed structural branch of the named domain explanation, not same type or complete exam-style practice. The other four property explanations are excluded.

Both differentiate an implicit product and isolate dy/dx. Q6(i) has the simpler affine product (x-6)(y+4)=2 and returns a general expression. The exam product 2e^(3x) y also needs exponential chain differentiation, includes y², and requires evaluation at (0,-5). Thus the named derivative subpart is an easier branch. The gradient calculation embedded in ii supports transfer, but the asked normal line is not silently treated as a gradient-only response; ii–iv are excluded.

Both substitute a point into an already available implicit derivative to obtain its gradient. The exam must first recover the y-axis point by putting x=0 in the original curve, then gives only its gradient; Q6(ii) supplies (7,-2), then additionally takes the negative reciprocal and constructs the normal equation. Source normal-line construction and target axis-point recovery run in different directions, giving a mixed branch. The derivative in source i remains a dependency; source iii–iv and exam derivative proof (a) are not added to the selected outputs.
